The mission of the IBAS program is to help modernize the defense industrial base to ensure the U.S. maintains cutting edge capabilities. Nuclear Focused: Many DOE labs across the country are focused on civilian and defense nuclear applications and production including Idaho National Lab, Los Alamos National Lab, Sandia National Lab, Lawrence Livermore National Lab, Savannah River National Lab, and contractors including Y-12, and Kansas City National Security Campus. There may be potential for collaboration of a centralized DOE electron beam welding and wire additive facility with these labs. A suggested location for this centralized lab could be either ORNL MDF, or a private contractor. One model for collaboration is DOE Project DE-NE0008629: Establishing Modular In-Chamber Electron Beam Welding Capability in the USA for reactor vessel applications [76]. This is project is being led by Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), a US non-profit organization, in collaboration with BWXT, PTR Precision Technologies, R-V Industries, and UK’s Advanced Manufacturing Research Center (AMRC). The project includes the design, fabrication, commissioning, and demonstration of a high power EBW system for welding >4” thick vessels up 10’ in diameter, with an example of the system previously shown in Figure 24. Multiple private companies are engaged to fabricate the vacuum chamber, electron beam gun and motion sub- systems. The equipment will be hosted as a technology demonstrator at the BWXT facility in Barberton, Ohio. Significant upgrades to the BWXT facility have been implemented to host this heavy machinery. This project is funded through DoE Nuclear Energy program as well as other public sponsorships and has included over 35 personnel from diverse backgrounds over a 6-year project. The DOE provided $5.1M in funds towards the total estimated project costs of $6.4M, roughly 80% of the total project costs[77] It is anticipated that this system can perform one(1) thick section girth weld per day and could be used for vessels, steam generators, pressurizers, large valves as well as Navy applications. The primary benefit of this system is significantly reduced welding times (up to 90%) over conventional welding practices as well as elimination of welding consumables and reduced heat-affected zone. While the DOE reserves the rights to the equipment following project completion, it is likely the equipment stay at BWXT Barberton once the project has been completed. Academic Collaborators: While several leading US academic institutes require electron beam welding for their research facilities, only 2 have electron beam welding equipment. Michigan State University has a facility designed to support accelerator development and low volume prototype development. The Ohio State University (OSU) recently received electron beam welding equipment suitable for advancing electron beam welding science, initial development of joining processes, and workforce training.
